claims.text:
At least two explanations exist for the name Ossë. In The Etymologies, it is understood as the Qenya word osse ("terror"), deriving from the root GOS ("dread").
A later note pertaining to the name instead suggests it is a name of non-Elvish origin, deriving from Valarin Oš(o)šai ("spuming, foaming"). The same later note mentions that Ossë's Sindarin names were Gaerys (also containing the S. element gaer "dread") and Yssion.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, Part Three: "The Etymologies", p. 359; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Four. Quendi and Eldar", p. 400; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Appendix: Elements in Quenya and Sindarin Names", gaer

claims.text: It was said that during the early days of Arda, Ossë turned to Melkor for a time, but Uinen brought him back to the loyalty of Ulmo. However, Ossë's wild and wilful nature was still evident despite remaining loyal to Ulmo.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Valaquenta: Of the Maiar"

claims.text: During the Great March of the Eldar to Valinor, Ossë was sent to befriend the Lindar, the clan of the Eldar who lingered by the shores of Belegaer on their way, and he taught them sea-lore and sea-music. When Ulmo returned with the floating island for them to resume their trip to the west, Ossë (who loved the shores of Middle-earth) did not wish to part with his friends; he persuaded some, like Círdan, to remain there, at the Falas and the Bay of Balar. These afterwards became the Falathrim.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Eldamar and the Princes of the Eldalië"

claims.text: As Ulmo ferried the floating island with Olwë and his Lindar to Eldamar, they heard Ossë's song and begged Ulmo to stop off the shore, which he did. Ossë fastened the island to the bottom, and it became Tol Eressëa, the lonely isle off the Bay of Eldamar. However soon the Falmari of the island longed for the splendour and Light of Valinor and wished to see their kindred there. Grieving, Ossë submitted to the will of the Valar and Ulmo, and taught them ship-building and offered them Swans to draw them to Valinor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Eldamar and the Princes of the Eldalië"

claims.text: With his master, Ossë often visited Nevrast and the feet of Mount Taras in Middle-earth, and many Sindar were concentrated to that place.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Beleriand and its Realms"

claims.text: After the First Kinslaying, Olwë called upon Ossë against the Noldor, but he came not, as the Valar did not wish to hinder the Flight of the Noldor with violence.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Flight of the Noldor"

claims.text: After the Valar pronounced the Doom of the Noldor, Ossë helped guard the shores of Beleriand to keep the ships of the Noldor from reaching Valinor. His storms had a part in wrecking all the ships that they sent, and only one Elf from among their crews survived, by the will of Ulmo: Voronwë.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Fifth Battle: Nirnaeth Arnoediad"

claims.text: In the Second Age he raised the island of Elenna (Númenor) from the depths of the Sea.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Akallabêth: The Downfall of Númenor"

claims.text:
In older versions of The Silmarillion as well as the Annals of Aman, Ossë and his spouse Uinen were Valar in their own right, and often opposed the will of Ulmo.
In Eriol's Old English translations, Ossë is referred to as Saefrea ("Sea-ruler"), reflecting his status as a Vala (Fréa).
In that conception, Ossë is the source of the name Balar in place-names such as Cape Balar, Isle of Balar and Bay of Balar, which he often visited, and from which all Beleriand was named.
Ossë had a large house in Valmar made by Ónen and Oarni from pearls with a flour from sea water and roof from foam. He lived there during congregations of Valar or when the noise of the sea tired him. In The Tale of the Sun and Moon, it was mentioned that Ossë had green hair and his beard was torn.
Ossë was also the name of a Tengwa similar to Roman c, which apparently had the value o. However elsewhere, this letter is named Elwë and has the value of e. In the Mode of Beleriand this letter instead has the value a.
His name Falman from the root FALA (e.g. falma "foam") appears in The Book of Lost Tales Part One.
